fields.meaning: Shall I do it? | Shall I V ~? | Vましょうか Shall we V ~?
fields.connection: Vます (drop ます) + ましょうか
examples: Shall we take a short rest here?
Shall I carry your bags?
Shall I show you the way to the station?
It's raining, isn't it? Shall we take a taxi?
Shall we go with water for the drinks?
Shall I help you with anything?
fields.explain:
Used with the masu-form of a verb (drop ます) to make a gentle suggestion.
When you mean “I'll do it for you”, add the subject: 私が・こちらが + Vます-drop ます + ましょうか.
Formal and polite; suitable in service/hospitality settings: ご案内し ましょうか。
If you just want to make an ordinary invitation, you can use ～ませんか; if you want to decide together right away, use ～ましょう.

Meaning: “Shall we …?” / “Shall I …?” Used to make a polite suggestion or offer.
Two common nuances:
Suggestion to do something together:一緒に行きましょうか(Shall we go together?).
Suggestion to help:窓を開けましょうか(Shall I open the window?).
Suggestion to do something together:一緒に行きましょうか(Shall we go together?).
Suggestion to help:窓を開けましょうか(Shall I open the window?).
Degree of politeness: more polite than “～しようか”, friendlier than “～ませんか” when you want to take the initiative to help.
A rising intonation at the end of the sentence conveys a soft, suggestive tone.
fields.notes:
In service settings, 何かお手伝いしましょうか is a very natural set phrase.
To avoid sounding pushy, you can add もしよろしければ before ～ましょうか.
Not used directly with adjectives/nouns; used only with verbs in the ます form minus ます.
mistakes: Wrong verb conjugation: ×行くましょうか → ✓行きましょうか.
Wrong nuance: when offering help, use ～ましょうか (“shall I do it?”); when inviting others to do something, prefer ～ませんか.
Leaving out the subject when offering help in an ambiguous context: use 私が…ましょうか to make the meaning “I will do it” clear.

rows: Inviting someone to do something together
Asks the listener's opinion; polite; less of an offer to help
<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きませんか。
A request, not a suggestion to do something together

examples: The plan is going smoothly. However, we can't let our guard down.
The price is high. However, the quality is outstanding.
The amount of data has increased. However, the accuracy has not improved.
I made an effort. However, it did not produce results.
That proposal is attractive. However, the risk is high.
There is a lot of research. However, the conclusions do not agree.
fields.explain:
Formal and rational; suitable for transitions, or for stating limitations/exceptions after presenting the main point.
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence with a comma: しかし、…
In casual conversation, replace it with でも/けど to sound more natural.

Expresses a strong contrast/opposition between S1 and S2; often used to counter an argument, add a limitation, or present an exception.
Formal, objective style; suitable for written language, presentations and news.
Not used for a strong “surprise contrary to expectation” (better: ところが); not as casual as でも/けど.
fields.notes:
“しかしながら” is an even more formal variant, often used in academic writing.
In journalism, しかし can open a new paragraph to create a turning point in the argument.
Avoid overusing conjunctions at the beginning of a sentence in consecutive sentences; you can replace them with が/一方で to vary the flow of the text.
mistakes: Using しかし in casual conversation sounds stiff; use でも/けど instead.
Confusing しかし with ところが when there is an element of being “contrary to expectation”; a common JLPT trap.
Omitting the comma after しかし makes it hard to read: “しかし、…”.
Using しかし to link a command/request in everyday conversation can sound too formal or unpleasant in nuance.

rows: <ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>。しかし<ruby>課題<rt>かだい</rt></ruby>。
Breaks the flow, at the beginning of a sentence; less formal.
A result strongly contrary to expectation.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。ところが<ruby>閉店<rt>へいてん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だが<ruby>十分<rt>じゅっぷん</rt></ruby>でない。

examples: It's already late. Well then, let's stop here for today.
It's started to rain. Well then, let's take a taxi home.
That's difficult. Well then, let's try another way.
The meeting starts at three? Well then, let's eat lunch early.
I don't have any cash on me. Well then, I'll transfer the money later.
You passed the test? Well then, let's celebrate!
fields.explain:
Used to sum up or make a decision based on the information in S1.
Combines naturally with volition/suggestion: ～しよう／～しませんか／～しましょう。
Casual speech; in formal business settings, prefer それでは／では .
じゃあ feels soft and drawn out; じゃ is short and decisive.
Usually comes at the beginning of a new utterance; avoid inserting it in the middle of a long sentence.

Changing direction/making a decision based on what was just said: “well then / in that case”.
Marks the next step in a process/action: opens a new part after concluding something.
Implies “if that's the case, then”, but conversationally, not as a strict grammatical condition.
Casual, brisk nuance; often used when wrapping up/closing a topic or starting work.
The intonation usually falls slightly after じゃ、, followed by a command, suggestion, volition, or a statement of plans.
Not used to raise a strong counterargument; for clear contrast/concession, use でも/しかし.
fields.notes:
じゃ can open a sentence to draw attention: じゃ、次は…
Do not confuse it with sentence-final ～じゃ in dialects (elderly/old-fashioned speech). Here it is a sentence-initial conjunction.
In chat, there is a repeated emphatic form: じゃ、じゃ、… to call for attention again; avoid it in formal writing.
mistakes: Using じゃ in a formal written text → unnatural; choose それでは／では.
Using じゃ for strong contrast → wrong nuance; use でも／しかし instead.
Omitting the period before じゃ、→ breaks the convention for linking sentences: it must be S1。じゃ、S2。
Confusing じゃ with ～じゃない (negative) → different function.
JLPT: recognize the degree of politeness when choosing じゃ vs それでは/では according to a conversational vs formal context.

rows: The “あ” is drawn out; very conversational
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり？ じゃあ、またね。
Well then (a bit more polite than じゃ)
<ruby>締切<rt>しめきり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>？ それじゃ、<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ごう。
それでは、<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
では、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>みます。
それなら、<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby><ruby>日<rt>び</rt></ruby>にしよう。

examples: I heard it's going to rain tomorrow. In that case, the picnic is off, right?
Applications close today? In that case, I'll send mine right away.
That concludes my explanation. Well then, please check it.
Are you ready? Well then, let's head out.
Well then, see you tomorrow.
You forgot your key? In that case, I'll open it for you.
fields.explain:
Natural in casual work settings, friendly internal emails, and small team meetings.
Used at the beginning of a sentence, after the listener has understood “that (それ)”.
Combines well with commands, volition, invitations, and closing remarks.
If you need to be more polite (customers, formal presentations), replace it with それでは .

“Well then / in that case”, based on the information just mentioned (referred to by それ).
Moves on to the next step, starts an action, or gently sums up in conversation.
Moderately more polite than じゃ, less formal than それでは.
Often used to end a topic, say goodbye, or move on to a new part.
fields.notes:
それじゃ is suitable for ending a call/message: それじゃ、また連絡します。
In many mildly polite contexts, それじゃ is still acceptable, but do not use it in formal speeches.
The sound “じゃあ” makes the sentence less abrupt and friendlier.
mistakes: Using それじゃ in a text with a high level of keigo → not formal enough; change it to それでは.
Missing the reference for “それ” (the preceding content is unclear) → the sentence becomes vague.
Confusing its function with それで (so → cause and result) → different logic.
JLPT: recognize the politeness nuance among じゃ／それじゃ／それでは／では according to context.

rows: <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり？ それじゃ、<ruby>解散<rt>かいさん</rt></ruby>。
More formal; used with customers/an audience
それでは、<ruby>質疑<rt>しつぎ</rt></ruby><ruby>応答<rt>おうとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>移<rt>うつ</rt></ruby>ります。
<ruby>遅<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>い。じゃあ、<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ろう。
Short, slightly stiff; used to lead a program
Clear logical condition, not just a transition
それなら、<ruby>後日<rt>ごじつ</rt></ruby>に。

examples: It's time. Well then, let us begin.
Thank you for your kind attention. Well then, I will take my leave.
This concludes my explanation. Well then, we will move on to questions and answers.
If there are no particular problems, then we will conclude the contract.
That's all for the main topic. Well then, let us move on to the summary.
Thank you very much for today. Well then, until next time.
fields.explain:
Polite, standard in business/academic settings; suitable for emails, presentations, and MCs.
Placed at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one; usually followed by a heading, an instruction, or the next step.
Combines well with keigo: ～いたします／～でございます。
If you need something short and moderately formal, consider では、 .

“Well then / Then” with a polite nuance, used to steer things to the next part.
Used to open a new action/topic after completing the previous part.
Closes a conversation, an email, or a meeting in a serious manner.
A proper, standard tone, suitable for business and academic settings.
fields.notes:
それでは often goes with set phrases when opening/closing a meeting.
In written texts, you can start a new line after それでは、 to emphasize the paragraph transition.
Do not overuse it; using it too much can feel “formulaic”.
mistakes: Using それじゃ instead of それでは in a formal speech → not polite enough.
Confusing それでは with それで (cause-result) → wrong logical relationship.
Omitting the comma after それでは makes the rhythm less natural; there should be a “、”.
JLPT: choose the right level of politeness for the context of a presentation/business email.

rows: それでは、<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
Short, slightly stiff; common in written language
Less formal than それでは
それじゃ、また<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>。
Cause → result; different logic from “making a decision”
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。それで、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>した。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。でも、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない。

examples: We will now open the meeting. Now then, the first item on the agenda.
Preparations are complete up to this point. Now then, we will begin the experiment.
That has already been confirmed. Now then, let's move on to the next point.
That's all. Then, this meeting is adjourned.
Is everyone ready? Then, here we go.
This is the problem. So then, what should we do?
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one; followed by the next part/action.
Suitable for minutes, slides, textbooks, and announcements.
If you want something softer/standard for speeches, use それでは ; if casual, use じゃ／それじゃ .

“Now/Well then/Then”, used to move to the next step and to open/close a part concisely.
Feels like coordinating or official business; not very casual.
Often accompanied by a heading, an instruction, or the next step in a process.
fields.notes:
では also appears in the conditional structure: ではない／ではありません; do not confuse it with the sentence-initial conjunction.
In MC scripts/slides, では、+ a heading noun is very common: では、まとめ。
mistakes: Using では in casual conversation → feels stiff; use じゃ／それじゃ instead.
Confusing では (conjunction) with それで (cause) → wrong sentence logic.
Omitting the comma after では makes the rhythm less natural.
JLPT: choose では when the context is a written text, a presentation, or an official announcement.

rows: Longer, soft; for speaking in front of an audience
それでは、<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わります。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。それで、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>。
さて、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ります。

examples: Japanese is difficult. But it's interesting.
I want to go. But I don't have time.
He is kind. But he is sometimes strict.
The reservations were fully booked. But it is possible if you join the waiting list for cancellations.
That is dangerous. But it is necessary.
It's raining. But we'll still practice.
fields.explain:
Opens the following sentence to present an opposing point, a limitation, or an exception.
Neutral → casual; in more formal writing, consider しかし／だが／とはいえ .
Usually followed by an affirmation of one's position, an alternative solution, or an exception.
Keep the comma after でも so the sentence reads naturally.

Presents a point of contrast/an exception to the previous sentence: “but/however”.
Conversational nuance, softer than しかし／だが, stronger than けど(も) when placed at the beginning of a sentence.
The rhythm “S1。でも、S2。” makes the flow clear and easy to say.
Often used when S2 expresses a volition/evaluation opposed to S1.
fields.notes:
でも at the beginning of a sentence clearly breaks the flow and is easy to use in conversation.
Do not confuse it with N + でも (suggesting “or something”/“even”). The context determines the meaning.
In formal writing, replace it with しかし／とはいえ／一方 depending on your intention.
mistakes: Writing one long sentence “…,でも、…” → spoken style; in written language, split it into two sentences.
Confusing “でも” (conjunction) with “N + でも” (suggestion/even) → wrong meaning.
Using でも instead of しかし in a formal text → not formal enough.
JLPT: distinguish でも／しかし／それでも／ところが by the degree of contrast and nuance.

rows: しかし、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>がある。
だが、<ruby>例外<rt>れいがい</rt></ruby>もある。
Soft; usually attached at the end/middle of a sentence
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりだった。ところが、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。

fields.meaning: Emphasizes that an action or event in the second clause takes place after the action or event in the first clause.
examples: After grilling it
After Hachi died, the Hachikō statue was built in Shibuya.
Shun came after Hana had gone home.
Why don't we go for a drink after work?
Would you like some coffee?
How are your travel plans coming along?
How is this soup?
Are you keeping well? / How have you been?
Would you like a souvenir?
fields.explain:
“いかが” is used in formal conversation, especially when speaking to customers or superiors, or in service settings.
Placed after a noun or a clause, combined with “は”, “で”, “でしょうか”, etc.
Polite, gentle nuance that shows respect for the listener.
Often used in situations such as offering food or drink, asking for opinions, asking about impressions, and introducing products.

① Used to invite someone to eat, drink, or do something in a polite and refined way.
② A more polite way of saying 「どうですか」– often used in formal communication, customer service, or with superiors.
③ Can be used to ask for an opinion or impression, or to suggest choosing something.
“いかが” is the keigo form (丁寧語) of “どう”.
fields.notes:
“いかが” = “どう” in meaning but shows a much higher degree of politeness.
When used with “でしょうか”, the politeness increases further: お味はいかがでしょうか。→ Is it to your liking?
Very common in shops, restaurants, hotels, or when introducing products/services.
This form is not used with subordinates or friends (it sounds distant and unnatural).
mistakes: Confusing “どうですか” with “いかがですか”:
✕ コーヒーはいかが？ (too casual → use どう instead).
○ コーヒーはいかがですか。 (correct, standard politeness).
Wrong context: “いかが” is only used when speaking to superiors or in polite situations.
Omitting “は”: ✕ コーヒーいかがですか → ○ コーヒーはいかがですか。
JLPT N5 often asks you to choose correctly between “どうですか” (casual) and “いかがですか” (polite).

rows: How is it? / Would you like some?
Neutral; used with friends and equals
コーヒーはどうですか。
How is it? / Would you like some?
コーヒーはいかがですか。
How is it? / What do you think?
Very polite; used in business/customer service
こちらのプランはいかがでしょうか。

examples: I don't know whether it will go well, but I'll do as much as I can.
There's plenty, so please eat as much as you like.
When the exams are over, I want to have fun as much as I like.
「You can eat as much as you like.」
「I'll come as early as possible tomorrow.」
I believe I did everything I could.
fields.explain:
“only” is neutral, without the negative implication of しか～ない; it can go with affirmative or negative statements depending on the content.
Particle position: だけ attaches after the word/phrase to be limited; it can combine with は/も/に/を/が for emphasis (それ だけは、それ だけを …).
VるだけV and できるだけ carry the nuance “as much as possible / as much as you like”.
～だけのN means “belonging only to / enough to ~”, sometimes “worth… to the extent that” depending on the context.

Limitation/Only: only N / only that much / only do V (limitation of scope, quantity, target).
Maximum possible: できるだけ／VるだけV express “as much as possible / as much as you like”.
Emphasizing a minimum/special case: ～だけは (at least / as for ~ in particular), ～だけでも (even just ~ is…).
Neutral nuance; compared with しか～ない, だけ can be used in affirmative sentences, while しか goes with the negative.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to take ～だけ only as “only” in the restrictive sense.
→ At N3, ～だけ very often expresses degree/scope: できるだけ, 好きなだけ.
2) Distinguish it from ～しか.
→ ～しか always goes with the negative and has a restrictive nuance; ～だけ is neutral and can be positive.
3) Distinguish それだけ from ～だけ.
→ それだけ often means “corresponding to that degree” (pronoun), not the grammar point “only”.
mistakes: Using だけ with a negative to give a “lacking” nuance like しか: “三人だけしか来ない” is a wrong overlap; choose either だけ or しか～ない.
Leaving out the emphasizing particle: to emphasize a minimum/special case, は/も is needed: それだけは言いたい。
Confusing “Vるだけ” (just do) with “VたいだけV” (do as much as you like): the meanings are different.
Misunderstanding “～だけのN”: it can mean “enough to ~” (この成績は合格するだけのレベルだ), not only “belonging only to”.
Confusing it with “～だけに/～だけあって”: these are different patterns; check the context in JLPT questions.

rows: Can be used in affirmative sentences
Must go with ～ない; nuance of lack/regret
<ruby>一人<rt>ひとり</rt></ruby>しか<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった
Can carry a nuance of too much/bias; also means “about”
お<ruby>菓<rt>かし</rt></ruby><ruby>子<rt></rt></ruby>ばかり<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる

examples:
A: What do you want to do now?
B: I want to drink some water.

A: What are you going to do?
B: I don't want to study!
fields.explain:
Vたい behaves like an i-adjective.
In the tai-form, the particle が can be used instead of を.
The tai-form is not used with the verb ある.
